source.title: Induction Meets Biology: Mechanisms of Repeat Detection in Protein Language Models
source.authors: Gal Kesten-Pomeranz; Yaniv Nikankin; Anja Reusch; Tomer Tsaban; Ora Schueler-Furman; Yonatan Belinkov

page_placements.theme: Conditions and limits of induction-style copying (token rarity, configuration, long repeats, divergence, direction)

record.tranche_reason: Conceptually tests induction-like aligned-token attention and copying in protein language models using circuit attribution and masked-token prediction, rather than the original training-dynamics setup.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test induction-head formation during training, training-loss bumps, in-context learning as loss falling with token index, or few-shot task learning. Its tested task is masked-token completion in repeated protein sequences. It identifies induction-like heads and measures their contributions to repeat completion, including under increasing repeat divergence.
record.test_reason: The study finds induction-like heads (aligned-token attention plus copying) in two bidirectional masked protein language models. They carry the repeat-completion prediction, which bears on V4's claim that induction heads appear in other architectures and modalities. It does not study training dynamics, in-context learning as loss falling with token index, few-shot tasks, or previous-token-head composition in small attention-only models.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that PLM repeat detection is driven mainly by induction heads and other LLM-like mechanisms (relative-position heads, repetition neurons), combined with biologically specialized components. The mechanism is shared by ESM-3 and ESM-C. The main difference is that ESM-3 uses secondary-structure-sensitive neurons, which the authors attribute to its training data. The divergence-weakening result comes from an appendix failure analysis.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes trained masked-language-model protein encoders using circuit discovery, AP-IG attribution, attention-pattern features, and logit-lens measurements. It does not reproduce the original training-trajectory or in-context-learning measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Induction-head attribution changes with repeat length and substitution rate; the reported drop begins at lower substitution rates for shorter repeats.

fits_no_version.finding: Induction-head attribution stays stable until a repeat-length-dependent substitution rate, then drops sharply: about 30–40% for length 10, about 70% for length 20 and 75–80% for length 30, in both models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In repeat completion, the contribution of induction heads degrades with divergence between the two repeat copies, and longer repeats tolerate more divergence.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: Mechanistic analyses are restricted to successful examples and repeat-completion tasks with exactly two repeat occurrences; approximate repeats are limited to up to 50% substitutions. Only two protein language models are analyzed. The study does not investigate training-time formation or in-context learning in the claim's sense. Several attribution trends are shown in figures without exact values.

untested.parts: Only two protein masked encoders are tested, ESM-3-open-1.4B and ESM-C-600M. Other families, model sizes and training runs are not tested, and neither is when or whether the heads form during training.
No small attention-only models are studied, previous-token-head composition is not tested, and the [A][B]…[A]→[B] autoregressive setup is not used.
Training data and setup are not varied. ESM-3 and ESM-C differ in training, but induction heads are found in both, and the paper does not test whether training affects their formation.

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source is this study. The induction heads here are defined by an attention/copying score in bidirectional encoders, and the masked token can attend to aligned tokens in either direction, so the match to the original autoregressive definition is functional rather than exact. Analyses use only successful examples. The reader's links of rows to V1 and V5 were removed.

versions.untested_parts: Tests induction-like attention between aligned repeat positions and contribution to masked-token copying, but not composition with an earlier previous-token head or the exact [A][B] … [A] → [B] language-model setup.
Tests two protein language models only; does not test a range of model families, sizes, training runs, non-protein modalities, or other architectures.
Tests how repeat-sequence divergence affects induction-head attribution, but not when heads form during training, training setup changes, or persistence of in-context learning.

rows.subject: ESM-3-open-1.4B
rows.operation_detail: Measured the induction feature score for attention-head clusters on approximate-repeat sequences.
rows.measure: Cluster-level induction score; authors define it from copying and pattern-matching measures.
rows.note: The authors identify this cluster as induction heads and report it has the highest induction score among the three clusters.
rows.check: Remove V1: ESM-3 is a 1.4B masked encoder, not a small attention-only model, and no previous-token composition is tested. Baseline is stated: the other clusters score 0.026 and 0.045 (Table 11).

source_check.correct: Induction cluster: score 0.650, 7 heads. Comparison clusters: C0 score 0.026; C2 score 0.045.
source_check.problem: The comparison-cluster scores are stated; baseline should not be 'not stated'.

rows.subject: ESM-3-open-1.4B
rows.operation_detail: Measured induction-head AP-IG attribution while progressively substituting the other occurrence of an identical natural repeat, leaving the token aligned to the mask unchanged.
rows.measure: Average AP-IG attribution to induction heads.
rows.value: Attribution remains stable or initially increases, then drops sharply; the transition is around a 30–40% substitution rate.
rows.note: The paper describes a length-dependent threshold and says the mechanism becomes less effective for short or highly divergent repeats.
rows.check: This row varies repeat divergence in the input at inference. It is not a training or data manipulation (so not V5) and not the small-model mechanism (so not V1). The threshold values are read off Fig. 10.

relationships.condition: ESM-3-open-1.4B and ESM-C-600M (bidirectional masked protein LMs), repeat-completion task
relationships.reason: Both models contain a distinct cluster of induction heads (scores 0.650 and 0.493 vs ≤0.045 for the other clusters; R1, R2). These heads are the first group to promote the correct token (R3, R4), and they have the largest direct effect on the logits among head groups (R5, R6).
relationships.display_finding: Induction clusters score 0.650 and 0.493 versus at most 0.045 for other clusters, promote correct tokens first and exert the largest direct logit effects.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: ESM-3-open-1.4B and ESM-C-600M (bidirectional masked protein LMs), repeat-completion task
labels.reason: R1–R2 identify distinct clusters combining aligned-token attention and copying in both models; R3–R6 establish early correct-token promotion and the strongest output-logit influence among attention-head groups.

relation.reason: Its own attention-feature, attribution and logit-lens results test V4 in protein language models.

tranche.reason: The study reports induction-like attention and copying in a new setting: masked protein transformer encoders performing repeat completion.

source_check.notes: Mechanistic analyses are restricted to successful predictions; ESM-3 uses only its sequence track. Appendix E explicitly states the approximate substitution thresholds, contrary to the pack's suggestion that they are figure-only; these are inference-time robustness results, not training transitions.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Approximate-repeat masked-token completion in ESM-3 and ESM-C
reader_labels.reason: Both models have identified induction-head clusters with measured induction scores, and the authors report that these heads promote the correct token first and influence output logits (R1–R6).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Increasingly divergent repeats in both models
reader_labels.reason: Induction-head attribution falls sharply beyond a repeat-length-dependent substitution threshold, so the contribution is not equally robust across repeat conditions (R7–R12).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The two tested protein language models, ESM-3 and ESM-C
reader_labels.reason: Both models exhibit induction-like head clusters and middle-layer induction-head promotion of the correct masked residue (R1–R4).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Substitution rates below the length-dependent attribution drop in both models
reader_labels.reason: Induction-head attribution remains stable or initially increases before the reported threshold, with the threshold shifting to higher divergence for longer repeats (R7–R12).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Short and highly divergent repeats in both models
reader_labels.reason: Attribution drops sharply at lower substitution rates for length-10 repeats than for longer repeats, indicating weaker induction-based completion under short, divergent repeat conditions (R7, R10).
